clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive demyelinating Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy caused by mutations in FGD4, which encodes frabin, a guanine nucleotide exchange factor.
Frabin activates the Rho-family GTPase Cdc42, thereby regulating the actin cytoskeleton and Schwann cell myelination.
Onset is in early childhood with delayed motor milestones and slowly progressive distal weakness.
Progression tends to be slow, and ambulation is often preserved into later life despite early onset.
Scoliosis and foot deformity such as pes cavus are common orthopaedic features.
Nerve biopsy characteristically shows redundant myelin loops (myelin outfoldings).
Motor nerve conduction velocities are markedly slowed in keeping with a demyelinating process.
It was originally delineated in consanguineous families, underscoring the recessive inheritance and value of a consanguinity history.
reference.pathophysiology: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 4H is an autosomal recessive demyelinating neuropathy caused by biallelic mutations in FGD4 (chromosome 12), the gene encoding frabin (FGD1-related F-actin-binding protein). Frabin is a guanine nucleotide exchange factor that contains FYVE, RhoGEF (DH), pleckstrin homology and actin-binding domains; through its DH domain it specifically activates the Rho-family small GTPase Cdc42, while its FYVE and PH domains bind membrane phosphoinositides. In Schwann cells this signalling coordinates actin cytoskeletal remodelling and membrane dynamics required for the correct wrapping and maintenance of the myelin sheath. Loss-of-function mutations disrupt Cdc42 activation and cytoskeletal control, producing dysmyelination with the redundant, focally folded myelin loops (outfoldings) that are the pathological signature of the disorder. The resulting demyelination markedly slows conduction and, over time, leads to secondary axonal loss and the length-dependent motor and sensory deficits of the clinical phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 4B1 (MTMR2) and type 4B2 (SBF2/MTMR13), which also produce myelin outfoldings
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 4F (PRX), another recessive demyelinating childhood-onset CMT
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 4C (SH3TC2) with early scoliosis
Demyelinating CMT1 due to PMP22 or MPZ mutations
Dejerine-Sottas disease and other early-onset demyelinating neuropathies
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies showing markedly slowed motor velocities consistent with demyelination
FGD4 sequencing or a hereditary neuropathy gene panel to confirm biallelic mutations
Nerve biopsy in selected cases to demonstrate the characteristic myelin outfoldings
Spinal imaging and orthopaedic assessment to monitor scoliosis
Developmental and motor-milestone history in the child
Pedigree analysis and enquiry into consanguinity given recessive inheritance
redFlags: Rapidly progressive scoliosis with potential respiratory compromise
Emergence of cranial nerve or bulbar involvement, which is unusual and warrants reassessment
Any subacute worsening suggesting a superimposed acquired inflammatory neuropathy
Respiratory symptoms suggesting weakness beyond the expected slow course
reference.prognosis: CMT4H is an early-onset but typically slowly progressive demyelinating neuropathy, and many affected individuals retain independent or aided ambulation well into adult life; orthopaedic complications such as scoliosis are important contributors to long-term morbidity.
pitfalls: Myelin outfoldings are not specific and overlap with CMT4B, so the pathology alone cannot establish the subtype without genetic confirmation.
The recessive pattern often leaves the family history unremarkable, which should not deter testing.
Slow progression may lead to underestimation of the underlying demyelinating severity seen on conduction studies.
Failure to monitor and manage scoliosis proactively can result in avoidable disability.
references: Peripheral and hereditary neuropathy reference texts
management: No disease-specific pharmacotherapy; supportive and rehabilitative care through a neuromuscular multidisciplinary team
Physiotherapy and ankle-foot orthoses for slowly progressive distal weakness and foot deformity
Orthopaedic and spinal management of scoliosis
Podiatry and accommodative footwear for pes cavus
Neuropathic pain management with gabapentinoids or tricyclic agents
Avoidance of neurotoxic drugs such as vincristine
Autosomal recessive genetic counselling with carrier testing and family screening, guided by consanguinity
